newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamists take the long view.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamists take the long view.

text.p: Turkey's Islamists, now forced into a tactical retreat, have nonetheless laid down a marker for the future and served notice on the country's ruling secularist elite that their time has come.

Necmettin Erbakan shattered a seven-decade taboo when he parlayed a plurality of 21.3 percent of the vote in 1995 general elections to become the first Islamist leader of the officially secular republic.
"The line has been crossed," said one Western diplomat. "An Islamist won a fair election, became prime minister of Turkey and the sky did not fall.
"It is hard to believe this is the last we will hear from Erbakan and his Welfare Party in general," he said.

Most of Erbakan's one year in office, brought to an abrupt end by his resignation under army pressure on Wednesday, saw little progress in implementation of the utopian vision of his Just Order campaign manifesto.
Despite near-hysteria in the secularist media, Turkey is in reality no closer than it ever was to the sectarian violence of Algeria or the strict Islamic Sharia law of Saudia Arabia.

Instead, say analysts, Erbakan worked behind the scenes to build a lasting political legacy, slipping supporters of the Islam-based Welfare into the bureaucracy and the security forces -- lifeblood of the centralised Turkish state.

And he has opened the door to the rising business class from the Anatolian heartland -- more pious, less Westernised but no less ambitious than the traditional Istanbul commercial elite that has dominated the state-fostered economy for decades.
"They have done little more than employ their supporters in key posts in the ministries of finance and education and the police force," said political commentator Bilal Cetin of Welfare's tenure.
"Turkey is mostly run by the political and military bureaucracy. This is their investment in the future," he told Reuters.
Erbakan himself expects a quick return on that investment. He also hopes to build on Welfare's deserved reputation for clean and efficient government at the local level.

"We got six million votes last time. If we had an election now we would get at least 10 million," he predicted on June 16, two days before he resigned to make way for a proposed "election" government to lead the country to early polls.
In the absence of reliable opinion surveys, it is impossible to gauge the electoral prospects of the Welfare Party.
However, a number of factors appear to augur well for the Islamists' next campaign.

Secularist politicians remain hopelessly divided, and Welfare boasts the largest membership and most disciplined cadres. They are well-financed by a network of like-minded businessmen and backed by Moslem-oriented newspapers and television channels.

More important, recent heavy-handed tactics by the army to hound Erbakan from office -- even close ally the United States was alarmed enough to speak out against a potential coup d'etat -- have cast him in the role of martyr for democracy.

"If elections are held as planned before the end of the year, it will definitely be to the benefit of Welfare," said political analyst Sami Kohen, predicting an increase to about 26 percent from 21.3 percent in December of 1995.
"Erbakan can present early polls as a referendum on democracy and against military (intervention)," he said.
In addition, a series of populist measures meant hefty pay rises for the big civil service and increases in farm subsidies.
Erbakan's own struggle with the establishment has spilled over into the country's boardrooms and business centres, pitting the old elite against provincial pretenders.
A list compiled by the army, and then leaked to the press, targetted Turkish businesses suspected of backing "political Islam."
Sigificantly, most are based in Anatolia where Welfare is strongest, well away from Istanbul and its Westernised ways.
One such business, the department and grocery mega-store Begendik built under Ankara's biggest mosque, saw its sales plummet 10 percent.
Another, the huge Kombassan Holding, had more than $100 million in assets frozen by a Turkish court. The company is based in conservative Konya, Erbakan's own constituency.
And food retailer Yimpas, from the Anatolian city of Yozgat, was forced to launch an advertising campaign to defend itself against claims it was sponsoring Moslem activism.
